cards.answer: A model with huge weights fits noise. Before we can charge a model for being “large”, we need a number that says how large a weight vector is. Different norms measure size differently, and that difference is what makes ridge and lasso behave differently.

cards.teach: Day 13: J(w) = (how badly w fits) + (how large w is). λ=0 gives OLS. Larger λ shrinks weights toward 0, trading a little bias for less variance. Ridge (L2²) shrinks every weight smoothly but almost never to exactly 0. Lasso (L1) can set weights to exactly 0 , so it selects features.
cards.prompt: Why do we need this idea?
cards.answer: Ordinary least squares only asks “how well do you fit the training data?” With many or correlated features it can fit noise using wild weights. Regularization adds a second question, “how large are your weights?”, and λ sets the exchange rate between the two.
cards.explain: MSE is the mean of squared residuals. A derivative set to zero finds a minimum of a smooth bowl. λ ≥ 0 is chosen by cross-validation, never by training error.

cards.teach: Build x^1,,x^20, standardize, sweep λ, pick the λ with lowest cross-validated MSE, fit lasso, read the three largest |weights|, then refit OLS on only those three because lasso’s kept weights are shrunk.
cards.prompt: Why do we need this idea?
cards.answer: A secret polynomial uses 3 of 20 powers. OLS on all 20 cannot tell you which three; lasso can, because it pays for every non-zero weight.
cards.explain: Standardizing a column subtracts its mean and divides by its standard deviation. Correlation near 1 means two columns are almost copies.

cards.source: HW7 prog Q1 and its solution notebook; Day 13 pp. 12–17
cards.math:
Q: Why not fit OLS on all 20 and keep the three largest weights? On [−1,1][-1,1][−1,1] the powers are near-copies (x17x^{17}x17 vs x19x^{19}x19: correlation ≈ 0.999). OLS’s weights swing wildly (±160, alternating signs) and its three largest name the wrong powers (x12,x16,x18x^{12},x^{16},x^{18}x12,x16,x18). Lasso charges for every non-zero weight, so it explains yyy with as few features as it can.

Q: Lasso kept more than three weights. Why? Lowest CV MSE picks the best λ for prediction, not for selection: two tiny extra weights (x5x^5x5, x20x^{20}x20) lower the MSE a hair. They are tiny, so the true three still stand out.

Q: Why refit OLS? Lasso shrinks the weights it keeps, so they underestimate a,b,ca,b,ca,b,c. Lasso chooses which; OLS on the chosen few estimates how much.

Q: Why standardize? The penalty charges every weight equally. If one column has a tiny scale, it needs a huge weight for the same effect and gets punished unfairly; on a shared scale, comparing weight sizes is fair.

cards.source: Day 14 pp. 2–12 (penguin ICA, Gini, car splits); HW7 P3; quiz7 reminder sheet
cards.teach: Day 14’s penguin game: copy a random penguin’s species as your guess for another random penguin. Gini is the probability that guess is wrong. Pure node → 0. Evenly mixed K classes → 1-1/K. A split is good if the sample-weighted Gini of the children is low, i.e. the reduction is large.
cards.prompt: Why do we need this idea?
cards.answer: A decision tree asks yes/no questions like “x₀ < 3.5?”. To choose the best question it needs a score for how mixed the labels in each group are. Gini is that score.
cards.explain: A class proportion p_k is the class count divided by the node’s sample count. A weighted average multiplies each group’s value by its share of samples.

cards.teach: Since the leaf predicts y= y, its MSE is the variance of its y values. Score a split exactly like Gini: weighted child variance, then the reduction from the parent.

cards.explain: A mean y=1N y_i. Variance is the average squared distance from the mean (here without Bessel’s correction: divide by N, not N−1).

cards.source: Day 14 pp. 14–23 (bagging, forests, importance); HW7 P5
cards.teach: Course definition: a feature’s importance = total Gini decrease from every split on that feature, across all trees, as a % of the forest’s total decrease. It measures how much the forest used the feature . It has no direction , is not a correlation , and is not causation .
cards.prompt: Why do we need this idea?
cards.answer: One deep tree overfits. A random forest averages many varied trees. Its importance plot is a popular “explanation”, and HW7 P5 tests whether you know what it can and cannot say.
cards.explain: Bagging: each tree trains on a bootstrap sample. Forests also consider a random subset of features at each split, then vote (classification) or average (regression).

cards.prompt: Gini impurity of a node?
cards.answer: G = 1 − Σₖ pₖ². Pure node 0; even K classes 1 − 1/K. Score a split by the sample-weighted child Gini.
cards.source: quiz7 reminder sheet; Day 13–14
cards.teach: Say it aloud before flipping.

cards.prompt: Ridge and lasso objectives?
cards.answer: J_ridge = (1/N)‖Xw−y‖² + λ‖w‖₂²;  J_lasso = (1/N)‖Xw−y‖² + λ‖w‖₁. λ=0 is OLS.
cards.source: quiz7 reminder sheet; Day 13–14
cards.teach: Say it aloud before flipping.

cards.prompt: L1, L2, L∞ norms?
cards.answer: ‖w‖₁ = Σ|wⱼ|, ‖w‖₂ = √Σwⱼ², ‖w‖∞ = max|wⱼ|.

cards.prompt: One-feature ridge / lasso weight (no intercept)?
cards.answer: ridge: Sxy/(Sxx + Nλ). lasso: (|Sxy| − Nλ/2)/Sxx with Sxy’s sign, or 0 once λ ≥ 2|Sxy|/N.

cards.prompt: Leaf MSE shortcut?
cards.answer: MSE = (1/N)Σy² − ȳ². Weighted by child share, like Gini.
